title: Nike’s New NBA Collection Lets Fans Shop Player-Worn Gear for the First Time
description:
Ahead of the NBA season opener on Oct. 20, Nike has just released “Standard Issue,” its latest pro basketball collection.

	The collaboration is set
body:
Ahead of the NBA season opener on Oct. 20, Nike has just released “Standard Issue,” its latest pro basketball collection.

	The collaboration is set to introduce a “new look for the league, reimagining how team identity and basketball culture are expressed across players, teams and fans,” according to a statement. The lineup features NBA’s full 30-team roster, with each team represented on a variety of gear. To further fan connection, players will wear pieces of the collection throughout the season, including during warm-ups and team travel days. Nike notes this is the first time fans can purchase the exact gear they see on their favorite pro athletes.


	The first part of the lineup is available to shop online at nike.com, NBAStore.com and select in-store retailers. The second drop will be available to shop online on Oct. 12, just ahead of the start of the NBA season. Current prices range from $55 to $130.

	From fleece hoodies to basketball shorts, every piece of merchandise is complete with an airbrushed version of each team’s logo. The New York Knicks, 2026 NBA Champions, are featured prominently, with 10 distinct pieces, all released as part of the first merchandise drop.

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					New York Knicks Standard Issue		

	
		Whether it’s Jalen Brunson or Karl-Anthony Towns, match with your favorite New York Knicks player both on and off the court.	
		
	

	In 2024, Nike signed a partnership extension with the NBA, WNBA and NBA G League through 2037. The brand’s other recent collaborations and campaigns include NikeSKIMS, Air Jordan 4 “Comic” Sneakers and Powerbeats Earbuds (with LeBron James at the center of the campaign).

	Shop Nike’s full Standard Issue Collection here.

schema.headline: Nike’s New NBA Collection Lets Fans Shop Player-Worn Gear for the First Time

title: Box Office: ‘Resident Evil’ Makes $8.8 Million in Previews, Biggest Ever for Series
description:
The zombie virus is spreading to the box office as Sony’s “Resident Evil” reboot is taking over this weekend.

	From “Weapons” director Zach Cregger
body:
The zombie virus is spreading to the box office as Sony’s “Resident Evil” reboot is taking over this weekend.

	From “Weapons” director Zach Cregger, the new and original take on the horror video game series has made $8.8 million in previews at the box office. It’s aiming to make $40 million to $50 million domestically this weekend, but some projections put it closer to $60 million due to positive reviews. The movie cost $75 million to produce, so it’s on pace to become a back-to-back, box-office hit for Cregger after his horror movie “Weapons” ignited last year with $270 million globally after opening with $43 million. In comparison, “Weapons” started out with $5.7 million in previews.
	

	“Resident Evil” will mark the largest opening for the auteur horror director and the largest of the video game series after it has run for eight movies. The series started out as a 1996 horror video game that has spawned several sequels, spinoffs and remakes, in addition to adaptation across film and TV. Milla Jovovich starred in eight movies, helmed by director Paul W.S. Anderson, across the 2000s and 2010s that were once the highest-grossing video game movies (until they were dethroned by the “Super Mario” films). Currently, the franchise’s biggest movie is 2010’s “Resident Evil: Afterlife,” which opened with $26 million domestically and finished its run with $300 million globally.


	In the new movie, “Weapons” star Austin Abrams plays Bryan, a medical courier who delivers a mysterious package to a zombie-infested town. It will easily take the No. 1 spot at the box office after last week’s “Practical Magic 2” failed to spark.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘Resident Evil’ Makes $8.8 Million in Previews, Biggest Ever for Series

title: Oscars: Poland Submits Paweł Pawlikowski’s ‘Fatherland,’ Starring Sandra Hüller, for International Feature Race
description: Poland has selected “Fatherland,” Paweł Pawlikowski’s post-WWII drama starring Sandra Hüller, as its entry for the Oscars international feature race
body:
Poland has selected “Fatherland,” Paweł Pawlikowski’s post-WWII drama starring Sandra Hüller, as its entry for the Oscars international feature race.

	The black-and-white film — which follows German novelist Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) and his daughter Erika (Hüller) on a road trip across Germany in 1949 — world premiered in competition at Cannes Film Festival in May, where Pawlikowski won the best director award.


	Written by Pawlikowski and Henk Handloegten, the film also stars August Diehl (“A Hidden Life, Inglourious Basterds”), Devid Striesow (“All Quiet on the Western Front”) and Anna Madeley (“Patrick Melrose,” “All Creatures Great and Small”).
	

	On “Fatherland,” the Polish director reunited with his longtime filmmaking team, including cinematographer Łukasz Żal, costume designer Aleksandra Staszko and production designers Katarzyna Sobańska and Marcel Sławiński. Though the film is set in Germany, the production shot mainly in Poland.

	“Fatherland” was produced by Mubi, Our Films (a Mediawan Company, Italy), Extreme Emotions (Poland), Nine Hours (Germany), and Chapter 2 (a Mediawan Company, France). It was made in collaboration with Circle One (Italy) and Apocalypso Pictures, with the participation of Arte and Pathé. Producers include Mario Gianani and Lorenzo Mieli for Our Films, Ewa Puszczyńska for Extreme Emotions, Jeanne Tremsal and Edward Berger for Nine Hours, Dimitri Rassam for Chapter 2 and Lorenzo Gangarossa for Circle One.

	Poland’s announcement of its official Oscars selection comes as the international feature race is heating up, with fellow Cannes favorites “Minotaur” and “La Bola Negra” being submitted for France and Spain, respectively. See a running list of all of the international feature race contenders here.

schema.headline: Oscars: Poland Submits Paweł Pawlikowski’s ‘Fatherland,’ Starring Sandra Hüller, for International Feature Race

title: ‘It’s Time for My Voice’: Jennifer Hudson on Reviving ‘Dreamgirls,’ Booking Tom Cruise for Her Talk Show and Writing Original Music Again
description:
Jennifer Hudson is changing.

	Her transformation might not be as dramatic as the one Effie White sings about in the second act of “Dreamgirls,” but
body:
Jennifer Hudson is changing.

	Her transformation might not be as dramatic as the one Effie White sings about in the second act of “Dreamgirls,” but the EGOT winner is beginning what she describes as her “next chapter.” 

	It all started in Salt Lake City, on the final stop of her 16-city summer tour with Josh Groban. During her set, Hudson would let fans vote on a song for her to perform. Selections ranged from her “Dreamgirls” showstopper “And I Am Telling You I’m Not Going” and her R&B hit “Spotlight” to her renditions of Aretha Franklin’s “Respect” and “(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman.” But as Hudson sat backstage on that July 3 evening, she decided to buck tradition. “I was like, ‘Can I sing this one for me?’” Hudson asked her team. 
	



	

									Ramona Rosales for Variety
	



	She chose “Invisible,” a lesser-known song from her self-titled 2008 debut album. In the power ballad’s chorus, Hudson sings, “And now I’m gonna live my life for me, ’cause this ain’t how it’s supposed to be. No more standing in the back of the line, ’cause I’m invisible for the last time.” She hadn’t performed the song in years, but as she belted out the lyrics, something shifted within her. “I got emotional in the midst of it,” Hudson says. “The song is nearly 20 years old, but it hit different, as the children say. And I can’t wait to sing it again.” 


	Hudson and I have been chatting in a cabana on a sunny Los Angeles rooftop for about an hour, discussing the journey from her shocking elimination on the third season of “American Idol” in 2004 — she came in seventh place — to winning an Oscar for her acting debut in “Dreamgirls” in 2007 and all that came after. “God always has so much more in store than what you could ever imagine for yourself,” Hudson says, grinning as a gold stud that reads “EGOT” gleams in the inner corner of her right ear. 

	God clearly likes full circles: In April, Hudson returned to “Idol” as a guest judge, moved to tears as one contestant performed “The Circle of Life,” which Hudson also sang on the show. She’s also producing the Broadway revival of “Dreamgirls,” sitting in on auditions as the creative team searches for the next actress whose life will change by playing Effie. Then she’s got her talk show, “The Jennifer Hudson Show,” which has earned 18 Daytime Emmy nominations since its launch in 2022. This year, she got her first solo nomination for outstanding daytime talk series host. 
	

	“This is the chapter of …” Hudson begins, hesitating, “putting myself first. I’m almost an empty nester, and I’m like, ‘Wow, I’m fixing to get a lot of time back. What am I gonna do with that time? How do you put that into yourself?’ I’ve been disciplined. I’ve crossed every t, dotted every i, and it’s like, but what does it feel like if you take up more space for yourself?” 

	I confess that I, too, am a recovering people-pleaser, but I’m learning that I’m the people I need to please. Hudson gasps. “I’m writing that down,” she says, grabbing her phone and tapping on the screen with her long, purple fingernails. (Her lock screen is a picture of her 17-year-old son, David Otunga Jr., surprising her with a Mother’s Day bouquet on the set of the talk show.) When she’s finished typing, she shares her mantra: “It’s my turn now,” she says, adding, “When we’re always pleasing everyone else, it’s like sitting at a stop sign and you’re letting the other cars go ahead of you. That means we’re stuck in the same place. Something’s gotta give.” 

	And in moments when that analogy doesn’t hit hard enough, she recalls a line of dialogue she delivered while portraying Franklin in the 2021 biopic “Respect”: “I do what I want to do. I sing what I want to sing. I go where I want to go.” (Franklin handpicked Hudson for the role shortly before she died in 2019.) 

	It’s something that’s been top of mind for Hudson while in the studio working on material for a new untitled album. The music is inspired by her romantic partner, fellow Oscar-winning musician Common, and her son, a gifted musician in his own right. While Hudson is perhaps best known for adding her flavor to anthems made famous by other people, she’s now focused on writing about what’s in her heart.  

	“I only write when I have something I really want to say, and it’s my time for my voice,” she says. She’s reminded of something she learned in the making of “Respect”: “Carole King and Aretha Franklin both told me, ‘Use your voice.’ That has never left me. And when I use my voice this time, it’s going to be with my words.” 
	


	Hudson is a woman of faith, which she credits for her success. “I feel like the greatest gift my mother [Darnell Donerson] and my grandmother [Julia Kate Hudson] gave us was making sure that faith was deeply embedded in us and a part of our lives,” Hudson says. “My mother used to be very quiet in her life, but once she passed, not a day goes by that I don’t say, ‘My mama used to say … ’” (Donerson was murdered in 2008 in a tragic event that also claimed the lives of Hudson’s brother, Jason, and her 7-year-old nephew, Julian.) 

	As a spiritual person, Hudson was quick to pick up on the synchronicities that kept popping up in her life during this “singing summer.” One of the first stops on the tour with Groban was Toronto, where Hudson spent a few weeks training to perform on a Disney cruise line when she was 21. A couple of weeks later, she and Groban were in Atlanta, where, in 2003, she auditioned for “Idol” with Franklin’s “Share Your Love With Me.” Then, in June, she brought first lady Michelle Obama to tears while performing “The Star-Spangled Banner” and “The Impossible Dream” at the grand opening of the Obama Presidential Center in their shared hometown of Chicago. 

	A few weeks after that, Hudson shed a few tears of her own when singing at Clive Davis’ funeral. Hudson’s voice rarely falters, but she could hardly make it through her medley of Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah” and Whitney Houston’s signature version of “I Will Always Love You.” That emotional performance mirrored the 2012 Grammys, when Hudson was called on to sing that ballad the night after Houston died of an accidental drowning.  

	The intensity of that moment at the Grammys can’t be overstated; after all, Hudson idolized Houston when she was a kid growing up on the South Side. (“When I was 7, I was like, ‘I want to win a Grammy, and I want to be a singer like Whitney Houston,’” she says, smiling as she thinks of young Jenny Kate.) So how’d she get through it? “My mama used to always say, ‘Jenny, you work really well under pressure.’” 


	Not every performance this summer had Hudson looking back; some forecast what is to come. For instance, in July, Hudson sang the national anthem at the World Cup Final in New York. Afterward, she ran into Tom Cruise, and mid-conversation, she decided to take her shot at booking him on the talk show, even though the megastar doesn’t do many sit-down interviews anymore. 

	“I was like, ‘Tom, could you imagine your Spirit Tunnel? What do you think they’re going to sing for you?’” Hudson says, referring to the pre-show segment where her staff lines a hallway at Warner Bros.’ Studio 1 and sings a well-chosen song to welcome each celebrity guest to the stage.  
	

	The staff started performing this ritual in the early days of the show to hype Hudson up for each taping. “And then I was like, ‘Shouldn’t we do this for the guests?’” she says. Today, clips of the Spirit Tunnel — featuring Zendaya, Obama, Aaron Pierre, Gwen Stefani and more getting their groove on — go viral regularly. 

	Turns out that Cruise was aware of the Spirit Tunnel, and he said yes to the idea so fast “it made my head spin,” Hudson says, adding, “He’s like, ‘I watch the show, Jennifer. I watch everything. I watched you on ‘American Idol.’” 

	Hudson isn’t particularly nervous about interviewing Cruise. After taping more than 100 episodes, she has discovered her superpower as a TV host: It’s her experience having been on the other side. “Because I get to be around a lot of celebrities outside of the limelight, I want the audience to see they’re human,” she says. 

	It’s a chance for people to get to know the real Jenny too — the talkative, bighearted person behind the powerhouse voice. “A huge reason why I wanted to do this is so I could be me,” she says. 

	Which makes sense since striving for authenticity is what leads Hudson to strike the right chord when she’s performing. “What comes from the heart reaches the heart,” she explains. “What’s real resonates. If you don’t put meaning behind it, then it’s just a demo of right notes.” 




	

									Courtesy of the Jennifer Hudson Foundation
	


	
		Charity Spotlight: Jennifer Hudson Foundation	

	For the past 20 years, Jennifer Hudson has supported youth programs in her hometown of Chicago, but last year, she launched her eponymous foundation to expand that philanthropic reach nationwide and give her more flexibility to jump in where needed. 

	“I love the babies,” Hudson says. “Anything I could do to invest in the kids, I’m all for.” 

	Naturally, supporting youth music and arts programs in underserved communities is a priority. “Music helped make the difference in my life,” she says, adding that she funded a children’s choir so that kids could participate in choral competitions like the ones she loved growing up. “Those teachings prepared me for what I do today.”

	Another aspect of the foundation mirrors her talk show segment “Everyday Heroes,” which spotlights people who strive to make a difference — from teachers and coaches to bus drivers, nurses and foster parents. “What annoys me is when people think the only talents and gifts are singing, dancing or something musical,” she says. “I love to say to people, ‘This is your superpower. What you do is special.’ It doesn’t have to be glamorous or in the lights.’”

	Hudson credits her late grandmother, Julia Kate Hudson, with teaching her the importance of taking care of others. “She had a heart of gold, honey,” Hudson says. “We’re givers in our family. My brother, Jason, used to feed the whole neighborhood. I just like making a difference in the world.”

title: Duncan Sheik, ‘Barely Breathing’ Hitmaker and ‘Spring Awakening’ Stage Composer, Dies at 56
description: Duncan Sheik, who had a pop smash with “Barely Breathing” in the mid-1990s but then found his biggest success — and multiple Tony wins — with the lo
body:
Duncan Sheik, who had a pop smash with “Barely Breathing” in the mid-1990s but then found his biggest success — and multiple Tony wins — with the long-running stage musical “Spring Awakening,” has died at 56.

	The New York Times reported that his death was confirmed by his mother, and that he died of organ failure. Sheik had previously been reported to be in critical condition in a Manhattan hospital.


	The death came shortly before the opening of a new musical for which he penned the score, “Memoirs of Amorous Gentleman,” an adaptation of Moyoco Anno’s manga graphic novel. The first preview is set for Sept. 25, with the opening scheduled for Oct. 15.
	

	Sheik’s self-titled debut album in 1996 reached gold status and generated “Barely Breathing,” which reached No. 16 on the Billboard Hot 100 but felt like it peaked much higher, as the single had a surprisingly long tail and lingered on that chart for 55 weeks. The song was nominated for a Grammy for best male pop vocal performance.

	With thoughtful compositions that reflected his Buddhist bent, Sheik found appeal among fans of both singer-songwriters and the gentler side of alt-rock with material that drew comparisons to high-cred artists like Nick Drake, Elliott Smith and Jeff Buckley.

	Sheik grew disenchanted with the music business and successfully turned his attention toward theater with “Spring Awakening,” which opened off-Broadway in 1996 before reaching Broadway later that year, where it ran for more than two years. launching the careers of young actors including Lea Michele and Jonathan Groff.
	

	The show won eight Tony Awards, including two for Sheik, for the score — shared with the musical’s book and lyrics writer, Steven Sater — and for orchestrations.Sheik was also rewarded for his work by the Drama Desk Awards and the Outer Critics Circle, as well as the Grammys, which recognized the show’s cast album.  

	“Spring Awakening” got a revival on Broadway in 2015 and is due to be seen again in an off-Broadway production starting in November of this year.

	Not everything he put his mind to for the stage went over as well. Notoriously, the musical version of Bret Easton Ellis’ “American Psycho,” for which he wrote a notably high-minded score, proved to be a Broadway stiff in 2016. Sheik’s other musicals included “Alice by Heart,” an offbeat adaptation of “Alice in Wonderland,” which found him reuniting with his “Awakening” book/lyrics writer, Sater. It premiered at the Royal National Theatre in London in 2012 and ran off-Broadway for two months in 2019.

	Other musicals included “Noir” and an adaptation of “Because of Winn-Dixie” that was performed in Arkansas and Connecticut but fell short of Broadway. “The Secret Life of Bees” was a critical success off-Broadway in 2019, winning the Outer Critics Circle award for the best new off-Broadway musical.

	Prior to an awakening of a different part of his musical career with “Spring Awakening,” Sheik followed his rise to fame with “Barely Breathing” with solo albums that sometimes veered into the esoteric, at least by the standards of his contemporaries, but which received solid reviews. Among his acclaimed follow-up albums was 2001’s overtly Nick Drake-influenced “Phantom Moon,” which had him collaborating with Sater before their shared stage work put them into the theatrical stratosphere.

	His other albums included “Daylight” and White Limousine.” The concept album “Whisper House,” from 2009, was turned into a musical that premiered at San Diego’s Old Globe Theatre. “Covers ’80s” was a 2011 album of interpretations of songs by Depeche Mode, the Smiths, Tears for Fears and other new wave artist from the era referenced in the title. He returned to original material with “Legerdemain” in 2015. His final studio album, “Claptrap,” was released in 2022.

schema.headline: Duncan Sheik, ‘Barely Breathing’ Hitmaker and ‘Spring Awakening’ Stage Composer, Dies at 56

title: Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Transformation Initially Took Six Hours — but He Convinced the Makeup Team to ‘Get It Under an Hour’
description: For his new film “Digger,” Tom Cruise transforms into Digger Rockwell, a wealthy oil tycoon who was not blessed with Cruise’s own good looks. In ord
body:
For his new film “Digger,” Tom Cruise transforms into Digger Rockwell, a wealthy oil tycoon who was not blessed with Cruise’s own good looks. In order to put on all the prosthetics for the role, the actor was originally sitting in hair and makeup for six hours — until he convinced the team they could do it faster. 

	Speaking on Travis and Jason Kelce’s “New Heights” podcast on Friday, Cruise peeled back the curtain into his transformation — which included sporting a fat suit — and how he made it “more efficient.”
	

	“The first time we did the makeup, it took six hours, OK?” Cruise told the Kelces, adding that he started doing the mental math and knew that wasn’t going to work with his schedule. 


	“I gotta sleep at least six [hours]. They keep saying I need more… but OK, that’s 12,” he continued. “Now, we have 12-hour days filming. So now that’s six hours on, two hours off with the makeup.”

	To streamline the process, Cruise said he showed up with a chalkboard and started timing how long it took to put each prosthetic on. 

	“I had a guy there with a stopwatch and I’m like, ‘OK, you see that time, six hours? By the time we’re done, we’re going to get it under an hour,'” Cruise said. “They were like, ‘No, I’m not doing that, it will never happen.’ I’m like, ‘OK, first of all, if you say no, you can’t do it, you will never get there. So can we agree that we’ll maybe make it a little less?’ So with each piece that was going on, it was timed and then we’d drill and practice.” 

	It worked, and they eventually got his makeup and prosthetics routine down to under an hour. “They were like, ‘What?!’ And they didn’t even know it, and they didn’t even rush,” Cruise said. “I like going into a system, studying it and trying to figure out how I can do it better, more efficient. The films that I make, I’m constantly going, how can I do it better?”
	

	Although Cruise successfully shortened his time in the makeup chair, the practicality of wearing the fat suit and prosthetics was still difficult. 

	“I’m sweating because I’m wearing these prosthetics. And the scenes, they’re long takes and the rhythm of it — you really have to know what you’re doing,” Cruise said. “But I’m sweating underneath, so I came up with all these different things, like cooling machines.”

	“Digger,” which premieres Oct. 2, is directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu and also stars Riz Ahmed, John Goodman and Sandra Hüller. Cruise said he’s been working with Iñárritu on the movie for seven years and was drawn to the project because of his artistry and “what I’m looking to challenge myself with.” 

	“I want to make a lot of movies and I love working with different directors, I love learning from them, seeing their stories, setting the table for them, giving them opportunities,” Cruise said. 

	His passion for this collaboration is part of why Cruise doesn’t necessarily want to direct himself. “If I’m directing, I don’t get to do that, I don’t have that experience … I want to learn and I like seeing their point of view on things, and I like mixing it up.”

	Beyond “Digger,” Cruise is gearing up for the sequel to his 1990 racing film “Days of Thunder,” which he’ll star in with Anne Hathaway.

	“That movie’s going to be fun. I can’t wait,” Cruise said. “Get me in that race car again man, please! 

	Watch Cruise’s full appearance on “New Heights” below.

title: Jay-Z Revisits the Ghosts of Lyrics Past in the Illuminating (and Possibly Too Thorough) ‘Jay-Z in 8’: TV Review
description: On “Renegade,” his 2001 collaboration with Eminem, Jay-Z asks, “Do you fools listen to music or just skim through it?” It’s a line he references whi
body:
On “Renegade,” his 2001 collaboration with Eminem, Jay-Z asks, “Do you fools listen to music or just skim through it?” It’s a line he references while retracing the contours of his decades-long career during “Jay-Z in 8,” HBO’s eight-part docuseries in which he sits down with producer and industry legend Rick Rubin to dissect both hits and deep cuts from his discography. People think, he says, that “this music is just all about glorifying the lifestyle or all about money and cars. It’s like, you’re not listening.”
	

	The question of whether anyone tuning in is missing the meaning behind the lyrics is purely rhetorical when it comes to “Jay-Z in 8,” a thoroughly technical yet often superfluous exploration of the rapper’s life and career. Directed by Rubin, the docuseries is set in Paris’ Palais Brongniart, where Rubin cues up songs, seemingly at random, that Jay then unpacks, often word by word. It’s a reinforcement not just of Jay-Z as a whip-smart lyricist but of rap as an art form itself, a medium for opportunity and introspection.


	Jay-Z has, of course, attempted a similar exploration of his lyrical acuity in the 2010 pseudo-memoir “Decoded,” where he annotated 36 songs and shared personal anecdotes. But “Jay-Z in 8” feels more interpersonal between artist and listener, as if he’s drawing a direct line to his experiences by revealing his hand, card by card. For as much of a public figure that Jay has carved over the decades, he rarely gives interviews — he did a total of one this year, and zero in the few years before it — so it feels particularly revelatory that Jay is willing to share so much, so openly, in such a bare and exposing format.
	

	It makes sense that he’d opt for such an exhaustive deep-dive on his work amid a year celebrating its breadth and impact. After nearly a decade of musical dormancy — he last released a solo album in 2017 with “4:44” — he returned not with new music but a string of celebratory concerts including a one-of-a-kind headlining set at Philadelphia’s Roots Picnic and three back-to-back, sold-out nights at Yankee Stadium in July to commemorate the 25th and 30th anniversaries of his seminal “The Blueprint” and debut “Reasonable Doubt.” By year’s end, he will have played another two shows at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium, all without so much as the whisper of a new project.

	And so Jay centers the conversation on everything that’s led up to now with “Jay-Z in 8,” meticulously picking apart the words that power everything from smashes (“99 Problems,” “Empire State of Mind”) and fan favorites (“Brooklyn’s Finest,” “U Don’t Know”) to much deeper cuts, some that Jay seems genuinely surprised to hear (“Don’t You Know”). For longtime fans, “Jay-Z in 8” is the pot of gold at the end of a very long rainbow: Jay dives into his verses, reciting them back to an awed Rubin, weaving in explanations so casually that it’s sometimes hard to discern where the lyric begins and explication ends.

	These moments reveal the genius of Jay-Z, whose life story is coded directly into the songs booming through the two speakers situated across from them. He walks Rubin through his writing approach, recalling how quickly he records his projects (“The Blueprint” took about a weekend) and how he prefers to concoct entire songs in his head. He zeroes in on turns of phrase and double entendres that even Rubin didn’t catch until now — “I keep one eye open like CBS,” for instance, is a reference to the network’s logo, but also phonetically sounds out to “see BS,” or bullshit.

	A barefooted Rubin is often dazzled throughout “Jay-Z in 8,” replying “wow” and “incredible” or simply meditating on what he’s just heard by closing his eyes and nodding. He serves as both a co-star and director of “Jay-Z in 8,” which is gorgeously shot in black-and-white and does a lot with the set’s simplicity. That’s in part because Rubin lets the camera linger at just the right time — at the start of Chapter 4, for example, Jay-Z speaks of reconciling with his estranged father at the behest of his mother around the recording of “The Black Album.” He describes the relief he felt at making peace with his dad before he died a month later; you can see the purity of emotion across his face as the camera’s gaze remains unbroken.
	

	To his credit, Rubin does ask engaging and thoughtful questions throughout “Jay-Z in 8,” often prompting Jay to think of his experiences in new ways. But “Jay-Z in 8” stops short of plumbing something deeper. Rubin has had a long relationship with Jay over the decades — he produced “99 Problems,” and recalls meeting Jay for the first time when he offered to switch seats with him on a cross-country flight — and the familiarity between them is both a boon and a bog to their exchanges.

	When they revisit “Kill Jay-Z,” a song where Jay raps about stabbing a record executive in the late 1990s and the infamous elevator incident where Solange attacked him in 2014, they merely skim the surface, briefly chatting about how it’s an exercise in killing off the ego. As they listen to Jay’s verse from Kanye West’s “Jail,” they talk about how West took issue with Jay’s reference to a “red cap” — a double entendre for the MAGA cap that West wore and also “cap” as a colloquialism for fronting — but nothing about the issues that exist between them today. Any interviewer with distance from Jay, or perhaps refined skills as a journalist, may have approached the tracks more directly, and some topics here feel like they’re weighted with unturned stones.

	What Jay is willing to share can be illuminating, and there are tons of small details to feed even the most casual of fans. For instance, he reveals that he initially wanted to put Mary J. Blige on “Empire State of Mind” but later went with Alicia Keys due to the piano on the instrumental; his feud with Nas dated back to his debut album “Reasonable Doubt,” which was supposed to feature him on a track until he never showed up for a scheduled session; he should have held “Public Service Announcement (Interlude)” for the project after “The Black Album,” and “Encore” would have been a better first single than “Change Clothes.” Much of this is explored in a standalone interview episode, where Rubin asks him simple yet effective questions like, “Have you ever been misunderstood? or “Have you ever been the betrayer?”

	There is so much in “Jay-Z in 8” that by the end, it borders on excess. Some song explorations here, particularly in the final episode, don’t speak to anything more than what’s being said on the record. A keener edit would have made for a smoother watch across the episodes, whose lengths range from 37 to 61 minutes. But this is Jay-Z we’re talking about, the same artist who released an album every year from 1996 to 2003. As he’s said before, listening can be a passive sport, but the reward is in the details if you’re just willing to look a bit closer.
	

	The first two episodes of “Jay-Z in 8” premiere on HBO and HBO Max on Sept. 15 at 8 pm ET, with two new episodes debuting every Friday.

schema.headline: Jay-Z Revisits the Ghosts of Lyrics Past in the Illuminating (and Possibly Too Thorough) ‘Jay-Z in 8’: TV Review

	No official premiere date for Season 5 has been set at the time of this publishing, but it will launch in 2027. 


	News of the cast comes just days after it was announced that Peacock had renewed the show for an additional three seasons, as well as less than a week after the show won all seven of the Emmy Awards it was nominated for this year, including the third consecutive wins for outstanding reality competition program and outstanding host for a reality or reality competition program for Alan Cumming.

	In the series, players are whisked away to a castle deep in the Scottish Highlands, where they must complete tasks and challenges to build up the prize fund. But hidden among them are the Traitors, whose goal is to eliminate the Faithful from the game and claim the money for themselves. The Traitors “murder” the Faithful as the game goes on, with the Faithful attempting to unmask the Traitors before its too late.
	

	NBCUniversal is already working to expand the franchise, with the new series “The Traitors: New Blood” having debuted on NBC on Sept. 17. Episodes will stream the next day on Peacock.

	The format was devised by IDTV and RTL. Cumming is an executive producer in addition to hosting. Stephen Lambert, Mike Cotton, Sam Rees-Jones, Rosie Franks, Tim Harcourt, Jack Burgess, and Darrell Olsen also executive produce. Studio Lambert produces.

title: Introducing George Jaques, the ‘Sunny Dancer’ Director and ‘Ballsy’ British Creative Being Called the ‘Tom Holland of Filmmaking’
description: Luxury fashion house Hermès recently hosted a special dinner in London to celebrate the 10th anniversary of Athenaeum, the production company founde
body:
Luxury fashion house Hermès recently hosted a special dinner in London to celebrate the 10th anniversary of Athenaeum, the production company founded by British multi-hyphenate George Jaques.

	While a touch pretentious, the name was chosen mostly because it “didn’t sound like a 16-year-old made it,” someone who, at the time, “couldn’t actually spell it,” he explains.

	A decade on and Jaques — now 26 (and hopefully able to spell the name of his company) — isn’t just enjoying a culinary honor from Hermès. This week sees the release across U.S. theaters of “Sunny Dancer,” his second feature as director and a film starring the likes of Bella Ramsey, Neil Patrick Harris, James Norton and Jessica Gunning.
	

	Amassing that caliber of names, getting a movie made and landing U.S. distribution is no small feat for any indie filmmaker, especially someone still so early on in their career. But “Sunny Dancer” is just the latest and greatest achievement for Jaques, who in practically no time at all has hustled, blagged and charmed his way into the entertainment world, becoming one of of the U.K.’s most exciting and buzzy new creatives — and one with an impressive and growing rolodex of collaborators and admirers drawn in by his infectious enthusiasm.


	This status was recently underlined by Hollywood, at a meal at L.A.’s ultra-exclusive San Vicente Bungalows set up by his manager with, of all people, Al Pacino and David O. Russell.

	“David just kept shouting that I was the ‘Tom Holland of filmmaking,’ which I thought was iconic,” says Jaques, still sounding slightly dumbstruck by the experience. Meanwhile, across the other side of the table, Pacino was telling him how “excited” he was to see “Sunny Dancer.” “He was such a supporter and seemed so impressed by what I had done — and I just felt that was so utterly kind.”
	

	Back on home soil, another supporter is David Parfitt, the veteran producer who won the best picture Oscar for “Shakespeare in Love.” In perhaps more British terms, he once described Jaques as the “kind of guy that’s beating up the industry.”

	“I was like, ‘Woah, that’s savage,'” says Jaques with a chuckle. “But I also loved it, because I was like, you know what, I’ve been quite unapologetic in my way of doing things. I really believe that if you don’t ask, you don’t get and the worst people can say is ‘no.’ You’ll be upset for a bit, and that’s important. But then you dust yourself off and you go again.”



	

					Neil Patrick Harris, George Jaques and Bella Ramsey at the “Sunny Dancer” at the Berlinale. 
									Getty Images
	



	It would seem, at least from the outside, that few have an asking-to-getting hit rate on par with Jaques, as indicated by both his “Sunny Dancer” cast and its U.K. launch, attended by Kylie Minogue. In classic Jaques style, he’d connected with the pop icon after managing to get backstage at a concert of hers shortly after finishing shooting the film. Naturally, for a special screening in London, he invited her along.

	It’s a skill he’s been perfecting since he first launched Athenaeum, when he somehow raised £4,000 ($5,300) in his local pub to stage “Dilate,” a play he’d written about teenage drug culture, in an abandoned railway arch at London Bridge. At the time, however, he had bigger — and hilariously naive — plans for the production. 

	“When you’re 16, you’re ballsy. So I called the National Theatre and said ‘I’d love to speak to Nicholas Hytner as I’d really like to put my play on here,'” he recalls. “And they were just like… ‘No.’ But I didn’t know that wasn’t the thing to do!”

	Even without the support of one of London’s most prestigious playhouses, “Dilate” — with a little help from Jaques’ builder dad and a small amount of stolen electricity from the Porsche garage conveniently located next door — was a sell-out. And this was despite the fact Jaques was simultaneously juggling being writer, director and star, his first year of high school exams and working on a market stall in Clapham selling donuts, pizza and sausage rolls.

	Two weeks after its short run ended, word got around, and Jaques received an out-of-the blue call from Sky’s then managing director of content (and later CEO of Sky Studios) Gary Davey, inviting him in for a chat.
	

	“I remember thinking, ‘What the hell is going on?'” At the meeting, Jaques was also introduced to Zai Bennett, now overseeing production for BBC Studios, and Anne Mensah, currently heading up U.K. content for Netflix. Thanks to Bennett, who he credits as a mentor, he also walked away with Sky agreeing to sponsor his already-written second play (this time about mental health and suicide, which he would put on in a “real theater”).

	Another early mentor for Jaques, who by this stage was already being described as a “budding impresario” in his local paper, would be the British actor Jason Flemyng, who he says has been a “huge part of my career.” Introduced via an estate agent, Flemying agreed to chip in £1,000 towards his second play off the back of a phone call and would later produce Jaques’ first short film “Silence” (written while he worked at a barber shop, made for “no money” and shot largely in London’s Wandsworth Common). “Silence,” about PTSD and “probably the darkest film I’ve ever made,” would world premiere at the Bahamas Film Festival (run by the friend of a lawyer Jaques had met along the way).

	“I went over with my dad and had the most wild time — I think I was about 18 or 19, in the Bahamas, with my first film, and I picked up an award. It was like… what the fuck?” Jaques asserts that he’s since insisted every film of his screen in the Bahamas.

	It should be noted that some major industry connections have come about via more underhand methods.

	While the Sony hack may have been disastrous for the studio, it was a boost for Jaques in his early years. Amid the rubble of highly controversial emails, he picked out the address of Sony Pictures Television’s head of international production Wayne Garvie.

	“So I cold emailed him and he was like, ‘How the hell did you get my email?” he says. “I told him, ‘I got it from the hacks, Wayne.;”

	Garvie — a hugely respected name in TV — has been “a mentor of mine ever since — I adore him and he’s been so kind,” says Jaques, who adds that they’re currently “working out loads of stuff we’re going to do together.”

	Of course, figuring out an email address isn’t particularly difficult. Having been comically rejected by the National Theatre’s front desk the first time around, a couple of years later — now with several stage productions under his belt — Jaques discovered the address of Hytner and dropped him a note.
	

	“I basically said: ‘When I was 16, I reached out to the National, but now I’m 18 and I’ve run my own theater company for a few years. I would love to meet you.'”

	Hytner, one of the most accomplished names in British theater, replied, met the teenager for a coffee, helped him land his first agent and allowed him to intern on a production of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” sitting in rehearsals and watching him direct. 

	It was around this time, while developing his first feature “Black Dog” (by now having teamed with Scottish producer Ken Petrie) that Jaques’ acting career began to take off in a major way. Having already had a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it part as a German WWI soldier in a trench in Kenneth Branagh’s “Death on the Nile” (“I lied and said I was fluent in German,” he says), at the age of 20 he landed the joint lead alongside Jude Law in Marc Munden’s experimental 12-hour live single-camera drama “The Third Day” for Sky, made with the renowned Punchdrunk immersive theater company.

	The wild-sounding shoot on a remote British island — filmed in the middle of COVID for added complications — saw Jaques “being buried alive” in a trench with Law and, in one scene, forced to throw himself “while in my underpants” into the freezing sea. It was a scene he had to redo several times, to the extent that he actually caught hypothermia.

	“And it was the most amazing thing in my career I’ve ever done,” he says. “I am so proud of the work because forever on, after that show, I was the boy that that got hypothermia and went through what Jude Law did for less of the credit!”

	Following “The Third Day” would come another lead role alongside another acting icon, this time Samantha Morton in Starz’s “The Serpent Queen,” playing the “sickly, dying” King Francis II. Then came Sky’s crime series “A Town Called Malice” alongside his friend Flemying (who was disappointed to learn he was playing his grandfather and not, as he had assumed, his dad).

	For all the back-to-back work, there were some splashes of imposter syndrome. Despite his tiny role in “Death on the Nile,” Jaques jokes that he was the “only one who didn’t go to RADA.” Later on, ahead of an important scene in “The Serpent Queen” he recalls freaking out and telling the showrunner Justin Haythe (who also wrote “Revolutionary Road”) that he felt like a “phony” who didn’t know what he was doing and “got here by chance.”
	

	In response, Haythe grabbed his young actor by the arms and told him: “George, I wrote this whole scene for you. Take the confidence we have in you and go smash it.” After he did indeed smash it, co-star Morton urged him to “go home and have a long bath with lavender oil,” advice he ignored the second he got back to the hotel, calling the other actors and heading out to celebrate.

	Following “A Town Called Malice” (sadly nixed after one season by Sky), Jaques began shooting his debut feature “Black Dog,” naturally persuading several of the creatives he’d befriended to join him, including the marine supervisor and grip from that very nearly fateful scene in “The Third Day.” Jaques also somehow managed to convince Parfitt — just off his latest Oscar-winning feature “The Father” — to come on board as exec producer. 



	

					Bella Ramsey and the young ensemble lead cast of ‘Sunny Dancer’
									Colin J Smith
	



	“Black Dog,” a charming road movie about two troubled teens driving from London to Scotland, screened at the London Film Festival in 2023, earning solid reviews. Suddenly many more people, and not just those on the receiving end of a ballsy email or phone call, were beginning to take note of its then just 23-year-old director. 

	Written while in the edit of “Black Dog,” “Sunny Dancer” — which premiered in Berlin earlier this year, opening the Generation 14plus strand — would take things to the next level. 

	A coming-of-age “cancer comedy,” the film follows “Game of Thrones” star Ramsey as a grumpy teen sent to what she calls “Chemo Camp” for kids in remission — where she eventually finds a group of misfit friends and a renewed lust for life (plus sex, alcohol, drugs and all the trappings of adolescence she’s missed out on so far). It’s sweet, joyful, deeply funny and also profoundly emotional — taking a sad subject but ditching the standard cliches by making the story about the kids rather than the diagnosis. 

	Alongside the top-tier cast, it also features a cameo by James Blunt and has a score written by Este Haim. All were charmed — and quickly befriend — by Jaques (who, while in the U.S. promoting the film, has been staying with recent friend addition Neil Patrick Harris). Haim has made T-shirts to help the U.S. launch, which is also being supported by Scissor Sisters, the pop-rock band having attended the premiere in London after their gig was cancelled. There are zero scenes in hospitals.
	

	In a more recent ask-and-get update, for “Sunny Dancer’s” London premiere, Jaques convinced distributor True Brit to hire a bucking bronco and a drag queen “who was doing the splits off every surface.” James Norton, returning to a shoot the following day, initially said he could’t try out the bronco for fear of injuring himself. “Cut to a video of James on the bronco going viral on TikTok — I was just like, I am so gonna get in trouble,” says Jaques. Thankfully Norton didn’t just avoid doing himself a mischief, but won the competition by staying on the the longest. 

	“James is hardcore!” says Jaques, who admits that, having been given some “lovely bougie clothes” to wear for the occasion, he was “too slippy” and kept falling off.

	The image of Norton on a bucking bronco points to another reason why the growing pool of creative talent that Jaques has lured into his path — legitimately or sneakily — have stuck around. 

	“I think people want to work with us and on our sets because we have a lot of fun,” he explains, noting that Ramsey said it was “the most fun job” of their life. “That’s what I want this industry to be. We’re not doing brain surgery. We’re making films, TV and theater — let’s have a fucking riot along the way.” 

	As Jaques enthuses, it’s “much more fun” being a yes man who might make things happen. 

	“I just want to get excited about the world and live in the clouds with people. And if have to come down to reality because I’ve got a fat no, then I’ll come down for a bit. And then I’ll want to go back up again,” he says. “Right now, I’m just so excited about the work we’re making next and the actors we’re working with — and how, as David Parfitt says, we’re just going to keep beating up the industry.”

title: Bill Hader on Why Young People Hate AI, Voicing Cat in the Hat and the Status of His Jonestown HBO Series
description: Bill Hader offered his thoughts on voice acting and artificial intelligence while teasing his next projects at the Variety Entertainment & Technolog
body:
Bill Hader offered his thoughts on voice acting and artificial intelligence while teasing his next projects at the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY, held Thursday in Los Angeles.

	Speaking to executive editor Michael Schneider, Hader was asked about his concerns about AI as a filmmaker.

	“A new technology comes along and everybody kind of flips out. Like, oh shit, a lot of people are going to be out of work,” Hader said. “I don’t want production designers to go out of work … those people are real artisans, and they’re amazing. If this stuff can help them, it’d be better.”
	

	Something the “SNL” and “Trainwreck” star finds curious about the emerging technology is how different generations have responded to it.

	“I have talked to younger people, and they seem to hate AI,” he said. “They’re not into it. I don’t know why, but that’s the vibe I get. When I got an iPhone, I was stoked on it, and I didn’t think about Steve Jobs, you know? But [young people] are very aware of the people making [AI]. They just know so much. They’re afraid that anything can be manipulated.”

	Bringing the topic back to the world of entertainment, Hader was adamant that artificial intelligence cannot rival the human creativity behind shows like “Barry” or new Emmys darling “Widow’s Bay.” “If it can help things, you know … but I don’t think so,” Hader said about using AI in the filmmaking process. “I haven’t seen anything yet where I went, ‘Whoa, that’s better than Martin Scorsese.'”

	Hader then mapped out his career post-“Barry,” the widely acclaimed HBO dark comedy in which he played a hitman who is bit by the acting bug. Hader also co-created the show with Alec Berg and directed the majority of episodes. Coming soon, Hader directed and wrote a psychological horror film called “They Know,” in which he stars opposite Linda Cardellini. And he voiced the Cat in the Hat in an animated adaptation due this November.
	

	When Schneider asked Hader how he approached voicing the iconic Dr. Seuss character, he quipped, “The same way I approached Barry.”

	The Warner Bros. animated reboot reunites Hader with co-director Erica Rivinoja, who worked on “South Park” with Hader almost two decades ago.

	“She’s just so talented, so I kind of just took her lead on it,” Hader said. “It’s such an iconic character that you just want to stay out of the way and do the best job you can.”

	Hader said one of the things that surprises people about voice acting is that it requires “a lot of energy.” “Everybody thinks you roll out of bed and you just do it. It is so hard, and you’re literally screaming for four hours, saying the same line over and over and over again,” he said. “‘Open the door! Open the door! Open the door!’ And they’ll go, ‘Could you give us another “Open the door”?’ and I just gave you eight versions of ‘Open the door!'”

	Hader went on: “It’s kind of mind numbing. And then you see it and you forget all about how exhausted you are. Genuinely, I remember doing ‘Inside Out’ and driving back from a recording session, and I was like, ‘I need to pull over and like just drink some water’ because I was my brain was just fried.”

	Speaking about his next move on the small screen, Hader brought up his Jim Jones series in the works at HBO. “We’re talking about doing Jonestown at HBO,” he said with laughter. “That’s not a joke. That is true.”

	Variety broke the news of the project in April 2025, reporting that Hader was developing (and would potentially star in) a project about the infamous cult leader. Asked about the status of the show, Hader said, “I don’t know. Me and Daniel Zelman, we’re kind of still working through that. It’s a very rough subject.”

	And for fans of the less rough subjects, Hader indicated he’d be open to doing more “Documentary Now!” with Fred Armisen, Seth Meyers, Rhys Thomas and John Mulaney. “That would be amazing,” he said about continuing the IFC mockumentary show. “I really enjoyed doing that show. That was a very funny show.”

title: 'Barely Breathing' Singer Duncan Sheik Dead at 56
description:
Singer Duncan Sheik
                          Dead at 56 ...
                          Grammy Nom
body:
Singer Duncan Sheik
                          Dead at 56 ...
                          Grammy Nominated for Song 'Barely Breathing'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 18, 2026
                            7:55 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
            Duncan Sheik -- a singer-songwriter whose debut hit "Barely Breathing" made him a household name -- has died ... according to a post on his social media.
      
    
            The post went up just a few minutes ago ... featuring a smiling Duncan holding his guitar. The first line of the caption announced his passing, which happened on Thursday.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            The caption reads, in part, "The world has a lost (sic) a singular talent, and deeply influential voice in music and theater," adding, "Duncan’s artistry touched many and leaves an indelible mark on the cultural landscape."
      

            The post notes Duncan was a father, husband, brother and friend ... and he will be remembered personally for his incredible wit, intelligence and "depth of spirit" he brought to those around him. A cause of death was not identified in the post.
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... the Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter had been receiving care in the intensive care unit of a New York City hospital earlier this week.
      
    
            Duncan broke onto the music scene in 1996 with his self-titled debut album. The album went gold in the United States ... and "Barely Breathing" -- the breezy pop-rock single on the album -- netted him a Grammy nomination.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            He released a few follow-ups in the next few years -- though none of them achieved as much success as his debut -- all while collaborating with Steven Sater on the Broadway rock musical "Spring Awakening."
      
    
            The hit show -- which took 8 years to write -- won Duncan two Tony Awards ... Best Orchestrations and Best Original Score. It also won a Grammy for Best Musical Show Album ... and helped launch the careers of "Glee" stars Lea Michele and Jonathan Groff. His new show -- "Memoirs of an Amorous Gentleman" -- is set to begin previews next week.
      
    
            Duncan was 56.
      
    
            RIP

            The new wife of Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband Patrick Clancy is speaking out ... and she's tired of all the conspiracy theories tied to her hubby, and the noise surrounding their relationship.
      
    
            In a new preview that aired today on "CBS Mornings," teasing Patrick's highly anticipated "60 Minutes" interview Sunday, Rachel Danis says ... "I don't understand how the story has been so twisted."
      
    
            She adds ... "I would hope people know that Pat is, as I said before, the most selfless father and supportive partner. And I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday. And I don't think there's anything wrong with that."
      
    
            As you know ... Lindsay's murder case has led to some online users creating conspiracy theories that Patrick allegedly framed Lindsay for their children's murders.
      
    
            In another teaser that was posted on Thursday, Patrick revealed he asks his late children, Cora, Dawson and Callan, for "help" ... and that he still talks to them "all the time."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We saw Patrick -- who testified in Lindsay's defense -- at home during the trial, and he looked stressed with Rachel. We've also seen them shopping in the Hamptons, and they were even seen with big smiles in NYC during deliberations for Lindsay's trial.
